title: Contents
summary: This table of contents for 'Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces' outlines the book's structure around virtualization, concurrency, and persistence. It covers introductory dialogues, CPU virtualization (processes, scheduling), memory virtualization (address spaces, paging, TLBs), concurrency (threads, locks, condition variables, semaphores, common bugs), persistence (I/O devices, disks, RAIDs, file systems, crash consistency, data integrity), and distributed systems (NFS, AFS). It includes front matter (preface, acknowledgments), references, homework, and asides/tips, with chapters, subsections, and page numbers.

title: Preface

nodes.title: Preface (intro)
nodes.summary: The preface introduces the book 'Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces,' an homage to Feynman's lectures, organized around virtualization, concurrency, and persistence. It describes chapter structure, problem-solving approach, and historical context. Key pedagogical devices include 'crux of the problem,' timelines, asides, tips, dialogues, and an index. The book emphasizes abstractions, uses real C code, provides homework simulators, and offers projects (systems programming or xv6 kernel) to learn OS concepts hands-on.

nodes.title: To Educators

For educators, it provides the book's website, purchase option, citation, and suggests a 15-week semester or 10-week quarter course structure, noting delayed concurrency coverage and teaching methods like chalkboard, handouts, and code demos, with available slides. It requests linking rather than copying online chapters. For students, it thanks them, explains the book's free online availability to reduce costs, and emphasizes citing original sources to celebrate contributors and encourage deeper learning, with a footnote clarifying 'free' means downloadable but copyrighted.

nodes.title: To Students

nodes.title: 01 A Dialogue on the Book

An introduction to operating systems then describes how a running program executes instructions via the Von Neumann model, and notes that system software makes running programs easy, handles multiple programs, shares memory, and enables device interaction.

nodes.title: 02 Introduction to Operating Systems
02 Introduction to Operating Systems (intro)
nodes.summary: This introductory text covers what happens when a program runs, explaining the fetch-decode-execute cycle and the Von Neumann model. It introduces the operating system as software that makes running programs easy by virtualizing physical resources like CPU, memory, and disk, providing system calls/APIs, and acting as a resource manager. It poses the central question of how the OS virtualizes resources, discussing mechanisms, policies, efficiency, and hardware support. It references background material, defines the OS's role, and mentions alternative names like supervisor or virtual machine.

nodes.title: THE CRUX OF THE PROBLEM: HOW TO VIRTUALIZE RESOURCES
nodes.summary: This introductory chapter on operating systems explains the core problem of resource virtualization, detailing how OS mechanisms and policies efficiently transform physical resources (CPU, memory, disk) into virtual forms with needed hardware support, and why this makes systems easier to use. It describes the OS as a virtual machine, resource manager, and provider of system calls and standard libraries. The text includes a code example (cpu.c) illustrating CPU virtualization, with compilation and execution results, and notes running multiple instances with Control-c termination.

nodes.title: 2.1 Virtualizing the CPU
nodes.summary: The text introduces operating system concepts through code examples. Section 2.1 presents a program that loops, uses Spin() to delay, and prints a command-line string, demonstrating CPU virtualization by running multiple instances concurrently on one processor, highlighting the OS illusion of many virtual CPUs, APIs, policies, and resource management. Section 2.2 presents a program that allocates memory, prints its address, increments a value, and prints PID, illustrating memory virtualization where each process has its own virtual address space.

nodes.title: 2.2 Virtualizing Memory
nodes.summary: The text introduces operating systems concepts: a C program using malloc to access memory, showing memory as a simple byte array where loads and stores occur. It explains virtualizing memory, where each process has a private virtual address space mapped to physical memory, demonstrated by multiple program instances allocating memory at the same address and updating independently. Concurrency is introduced as problems arising from juggling many things at once within a program or the OS, noting that the OS runs processes concurrently, leading to deep issues.

nodes.title: 2.3 Concurrency
key_items: THE CRUX OF THE PROBLEM: HOW TO BUILD CORRECT CONCURRENT PROGRAMS
nodes.summary: The text introduces three major operating system themes: virtualization, concurrency, and persistence. It explains how the OS virtualizes memory, giving each process a private address space mapped to physical memory. Concurrency is illustrated with a multi-threaded program where shared counter increments lead to incorrect results due to non-atomic operations, highlighting the need for synchronization. Persistence is discussed through I/O and file systems, showing how data is stored reliably on disks and shared across processes, with an example of writing to a file.

nodes.title: 2.4 Persistence
key_items: THE CRUX OF THE PROBLEM: HOW TO STORE DATA PERSISTENTLY
nodes.summary: The text covers persistence as an OS theme, including volatile memory, I/O devices, file systems, and a code example for file I/O. It explains system calls (open, write, close), OS disk management challenges, performance techniques like write batching, and reliability protocols such as journaling. It also outlines OS design goals: abstractions for usability, high performance with minimal overhead, protection through isolation, and reliability despite complexity.

nodes.title: 2.5 Design Goals
nodes.summary: The text introduces operating system design goals and history. It covers design goals like building abstractions for usability, high performance by minimizing time and space overheads, protection and isolation between applications and OS, reliability for continuous operation, energy efficiency, security, and mobility. It then briefly traces OS history from early systems as libraries supporting batch processing to OS taking a central role including protection of privileged OS code.

nodes.title: 2.6 Some History

It highlights UNIX's importance and Linux's rise, and concludes with a summary of covered topics (virtualization, concurrency, persistence) and omitted areas like networking and graphics.

title: Part I - Virtualization

nodes.title: Part I
nodes.summary: A dialogue between a professor and student introduces virtualization as the first of three OS topics. Using a peach analogy, it explains that a single physical resource is shared to create an illusion of many virtual ones for multiple users, who mostly don't notice sharing. The discussion shifts to a concrete example of a single physical CPU being virtualized into multiple virtual CPUs for applications.

nodes.title: 03 A Dialogue on Virtualization
nodes.summary: A dialogue between a professor and student explains virtualization using a peach analogy: multiple virtual resources are created from one physical resource. The professor then applies this to CPU virtualization, where a single CPU is made to appear as many virtual CPUs to applications, enabling concurrent execution. The text introduces the process abstraction as a running program, noting systems may run many processes. It poses the challenge of providing the illusion of many CPUs via time sharing, and mentions OS mechanisms and high-level intelligence needed for effective virtualization.

nodes.title: 04 The Abstraction - The Process
THE CRUX OF THE PROBLEM: HOW TO PROVIDE THE ILLUSION OF MANY CPUS?
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces the process as the OS's fundamental abstraction, defined as a running program. It explains the OS's challenge of providing the illusion of many CPUs through virtualization and time sharing, distinguishing low-level mechanisms (e.g., context switches) from high-level policies (e.g., scheduling). It then details the process abstraction, describing a process's machine state, including its memory (address space) and registers, such as the program counter.

nodes.title: TIP: USE TIME SHARING (AND SPACE SHARING)
nodes.summary: The text explains abstraction in OS as involving time sharing (resource used briefly by entities sequentially) and space sharing (resource divided spatially, e.g., disk blocks), referencing context switches on CPU. It covers policies as decision-making algorithms for scheduling, using historical data, workload knowledge, and performance metrics. It defines a process as a running program, and describes its machine state: memory (address space holding instructions and data), registers (including the program counter).

nodes.title: 4.1 The Abstraction: A Process
nodes.summary: The text explains time sharing and space sharing for resource management, including context switching and OS policies. It defines a process as a running program with machine state: memory (address space), registers (including PC, stack, frame pointers), and I/O information. It discusses separating policy from mechanism and lists process API components: create, destroy, wait, miscellaneous control (suspend/resume), and status.

nodes.title: 4.2 Process API
nodes.summary: The text explains separating high-level policies from low-level mechanisms in operating systems as a modular design principle. It lists essential process APIs: create, destroy, wait, miscellaneous control, and status. It details process creation, including loading a program's code and static data from disk into memory, and contrasts eager versus lazy loading.

nodes.title: 4.3 Process Creation: A Little More Detail
nodes.summary: This text explains how a program becomes a process. The OS loads code and static data from disk into memory, lazily or eagerly. It then allocates and initializes the stack with argc/argv, allocates a heap for dynamic allocations, and sets up I/O with default file descriptors. Finally, it jumps to main() to start execution. The text also defines three process states: running (executing), ready (runnable but not chosen), and blocked (waiting for an event like I/O).

nodes.title: 4.4 Process States
nodes.summary: The text describes the OS's steps to prepare a process: allocating and initializing memory for the stack (with argc/argv) and heap (for malloc/free), and setting up I/O with default file descriptors. It then explains three process states—running, ready, blocked—and transitions between them, illustrated with CPU-only and CPU-I/O examples. The OS tracks processes via data structures like the process list and register context for context switching, as seen in xv6, to manage scheduling and state changes.

nodes.title: 4.5 Data Structures
nodes.summary: The text explains process state tracing with CPU and I/O, detailing Process0's I/O block, Process1's execution, and I/O completion, plus OS scheduling decisions. It covers OS data structures like process lists, the xv6 proc structure with register context, process states (including zombie), and context switching. Additional details include the parent's wait() call for cleanup and Process Control Block (PCB) terminology. The summary introduces the process as a fundamental OS abstraction, emphasizing mechanisms and policies for CPU virtualization.

nodes.title: 4.6 Summary

It outlines moving from mechanisms to policies for CPU virtualization. nodes.title: 05 Interlude - Process API
ASIDE: INTERLUDES
CRUX: HOW TO CREATE AND CONTROL PROCESSES
nodes.summary: The interlude introduces practical systems aspects, focusing on OS APIs. It discusses UNIX process creation via fork() and exec(), and wait() for synchronization. It poses a crux on designing interfaces for process creation and control. It describes the fork() system call as unusual and includes a code example (Figure 5.1), encouraging readers to run it.

nodes.title: 5.1 The fork() System Call
nodes.summary: This interlude covers UNIX process creation and control APIs. It introduces the crux of how to create and control processes, then explains the fork() system call, which creates a nearly identical child process, with examples showing non-deterministic output due to CPU scheduling. It then describes the wait() system call (and waitpid()), allowing a parent to wait for a child to finish, with code examples. The text emphasizes practical system programming, PID usage, and return value differences between parent and child.

nodes.title: 5.2 The wait() System Call
nodes.summary: This text covers process API concepts using fork(), wait(), and exec(). It presents a code example demonstrating fork() to create a child process, noting non-deterministic output due to CPU scheduling. It then explains how wait() makes the parent wait for the child, ensuring deterministic output. Finally, it introduces exec() variants, showing execvp() to run a different program (wc), with example output. The text includes code snippets, output traces, and brief commentary on determinism and system call behavior.

nodes.title: 5.3 Finally, The exec() System Call
nodes.summary: The text explains the process API in operating systems, focusing on wait(), exec(), and fork(). It shows how wait() makes parent-child output deterministic by delaying the parent until the child exits. It introduces exec() as a system call to replace the current program with a new one, illustrated with code that runs 'wc' on 'p3.c'. The text notes exec() variants and that a successful exec() never returns. Finally, it motivates the fork()/exec() separation for building UNIX shells, allowing environment modification before execution.

nodes.title: 5.4 Why? Motivating The API
nodes.summary: This text covers UNIX process API fundamentals, including fork(), exec(), and wait(), with code examples (p3.c, p4.c). It explains how exec() replaces a process's memory and why fork() and exec() are separate to enable shell features like I/O redirection. It discusses implementing redirection by closing STDOUT and opening a file, how pipes connect processes, and Lampson's Law. It also briefly mentions other APIs like kill() and signals, command-line tools (ps, top), and recommends reading man pages and Stevens/Rago for further study.

nodes.title: 06 Mechanism - Limited Direct Execution
THE CRUX: HOW TO EFFICIENTLY VIRTUALIZE THE CPU WITH CONTROL
nodes.summary: The text introduces CPU virtualization via time sharing, explaining the need to share the physical CPU among processes. It identifies two main challenges: performance (minimizing overhead) and control (preventing processes from monopolizing the CPU or accessing restricted information). It emphasizes that both hardware and OS support are required. The crux is efficiently virtualizing the CPU while retaining control. It then presents limited direct execution as a basic technique, describing how the OS starts a program by creating a process, allocating memory, loading code, and jumping to its entry point.

nodes.title: 6.1 Basic Technique: Limited Direct Execution
nodes.summary: The text introduces CPU virtualization via time sharing and the Limited Direct Execution technique. It outlines challenges of performance and control, emphasizing efficient virtualization with hardware and OS support. It describes the basic direct execution protocol, including process creation, memory allocation, and execution, noting problems like restricted operations. The section raises key questions about preventing unwanted actions and switching processes, explaining the need for limits to maintain OS control while allowing processes to perform restricted operations like I/O without complete system control.

nodes.title: 6.2 Problem #1: Restricted Operations
key_items: THE CRUX: HOW TO PERFORM RESTRICTED OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: This text explains Limited Direct Execution (LDE) for CPU virtualization, covering the direct execution protocol and its two main problems. First, restricted operations: without limits, programs could misuse resources; solution involves user/kernel modes, system calls via trap instructions, and trap tables initialized at boot. Second, switching between processes: the OS cannot regain CPU control if not running; cooperative approach relies on processes making system calls. The LDE protocol details boot-time trap table setup and runtime process execution with kernel stack handling.

nodes.title: 6.3 Problem #2: Switching Between Processes
6.3 Problem #2: Switching Between Processes (intro)
nodes.summary: The text discusses Limited Direct Execution (LDE) mechanism, detailing its two phases: kernel initialization of trap table at boot time and process execution setup. It covers system calls and return-from-trap, then addresses the challenge of switching between processes. It explains the cooperative approach where OS waits for system calls or traps, and the non-cooperative approach using timer interrupts to regain CPU control. It also includes tips on dealing with application misbehavior and highlights the crux of regaining CPU control.

nodes.title: TIP: DEALING WITH APPLICATION MISBEHAVIOR
nodes.summary: The text explains how operating systems handle misbehaving processes through limited direct execution, terminating them on illegal actions or traps. It discusses cooperative scheduling where OS regains control via system calls or illegal operations, but notes the limitation of infinite loops. The crux is how to gain control without cooperation, solved by a timer interrupt: a hardware timer raises interrupts periodically, halting the current process and allowing the OS to regain CPU control and switch processes.

nodes.title: THE CRUX: HOW TO GAIN CONTROL WITHOUT COOPERATION
nodes.summary: The text explains how operating systems handle misbehaving processes, using limited direct execution. Cooperative approaches rely on system calls or illegal operations to regain CPU control, but non-cooperative processes require a timer interrupt to preempt them. It details the timer interrupt mechanism, its setup at boot, and its role in maintaining OS control. Finally, it introduces context switching, describing how the OS saves and restores process state to switch between processes.

nodes.title: TIP: USE THE TIMER INTERRUPT TO REGAIN CONTROL
nodes.summary: The text explains limited direct execution via timer interrupts, detailing boot-time OS initialization of trap tables and timer privileges, hardware state saving during interrupts, and scheduler decisions for context switches. It describes context switch mechanics including saving/restoring registers via kernel stacks and process structures, referencing xv6 assembly code and a protocol timeline. It also addresses concurrency concerns when interrupts occur during kernel handling, deferring detailed discussion.

nodes.title: 6.4 Worried About Concurrency?

nodes.title: 07 Scheduling - Introduction
THE CRUX: HOW TO DEVELOP SCHEDULING POLICY
nodes.summary: The text introduces CPU scheduling, contrasting low-level mechanisms like context switching with high-level OS policies. It notes scheduling predates computers, originating in operations management, and poses the crux: how to develop a scheduling framework, including key assumptions, metrics, and early approaches. It then begins discussing workload assumptions, acknowledging they are unrealistic but will be relaxed later.

nodes.title: 7.1 Workload Assumptions
nodes.summary: This text introduces operating system scheduling, contrasting low-level mechanisms with high-level policies. It poses the crux of developing scheduling policy, covering key assumptions, metrics, and early approaches. Section 7.1 lists five workload assumptions: equal job runtimes, simultaneous arrival, run-to-completion, CPU-only usage, and known runtimes. Section 7.2 defines turnaround time as a primary performance metric and mentions fairness via Jain's Fairness Index, noting their trade-off. Section 7.3 begins describing First In, First Out (FIFO) scheduling.

nodes.title: 7.2 Scheduling Metrics
nodes.summary: The text introduces scheduling with five assumptions about jobs: equal run time, simultaneous arrival, run to completion, no I/O, and known run time, noting the last is unrealistic. It defines turnaround time as completion minus arrival (simplified to completion when arrival is zero) and mentions fairness, often conflicting with performance. Finally, it introduces First In, First Out (FIFO) or First Come, First Served (FCFS) scheduling.

nodes.title: 7.3 First In, First Out (FIFO)
nodes.summary: This text introduces scheduling with five process assumptions: equal runtimes, simultaneous arrival, non-preemptive completion, CPU-only usage, and known runtimes. It defines the turnaround time metric and contrasts performance with fairness. FIFO scheduling is explained with examples, showing poor performance due to the convoy effect when jobs have varying lengths. Shortest Job First (SJF) is presented as an optimal solution under the given assumptions, reducing average turnaround time significantly.

nodes.title: 7.4 Shortest Job First (SJF)
nodes.summary: This text introduces scheduling, focusing on Shortest Job First (SJF) as a general principle to reduce turnaround time, illustrated with grocery store lines and job examples. SJF runs the shortest job first, improving average turnaround time and being optimal when jobs arrive simultaneously. However, with late arrivals, SJF becomes non-preemptive and suffers the convoy problem. The text then introduces Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF), a preemptive approach that allows the scheduler to preempt running jobs to run newly arrived shorter jobs, addressing SJF's limitations.

nodes.title: ASIDE: PREEMPTIVE SCHEDULERS
nodes.summary: This text introduces scheduling, contrasting non-preemptive batch schedulers with modern preemptive ones that use context switching. It then discusses Shortest Job First (SJF) with late-arriving jobs, illustrating a convoy problem where short jobs wait for a long job, leading to poor turnaround time. To address this, it proposes relaxing the assumption that jobs run to completion by introducing preemption, leading to Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF), which allows the scheduler to preempt running jobs to improve scheduling.

nodes.title: 7.5 Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF)
nodes.summary: The text contrasts non-preemptive and preemptive schedulers, explaining that modern schedulers use context switching. It discusses Shortest Job First (SJF) with late arrivals causing convoy problems, then introduces Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF) as a preemptive version that improves turnaround time. A new metric, response time, is defined, and STCF is noted to be poor for response time and interactivity in time-shared systems.

nodes.title: 7.6 A New Metric: Response Time
nodes.summary: This text introduces Shortest Time-to-Completion First (STCF), a preemptive SJF scheduler that optimally minimizes turnaround time by preempting running jobs for shorter remaining ones. It then defines response time as time from arrival to first scheduling, noting STCF performs poorly on this metric. Round Robin (RR) scheduling is presented as a solution, using time slicing to improve response time and interactivity, with its performance dependent on the time slice length, which involves trade-offs with context-switching overhead.

nodes.title: 7.7 Round Robin
nodes.summary: The text introduces Round Robin (RR) scheduling to improve response time over SJF, explaining time-slicing, quantum length, and context-switch trade-offs. It compares RR and SJF on response and turnaround times, discussing fairness versus efficiency. It introduces amortization to reduce context-switch costs, notes on-chip state overhead, and describes overlapping operations for utilization. Finally, it addresses incorporating I/O by treating sub-jobs as independent and illustrating poor resource use with an STCF example.

nodes.title: 7.8 Incorporating I/O
nodes.summary: The text introduces scheduling basics, emphasizing overlap to boost utilization during I/O. It covers incorporating I/O: treating each CPU burst as a job, using STCF to run short bursts, enabling overlap and better resource use. The example of jobs A and B illustrates poor versus improved scheduling. It then discusses removing the oracle assumption—since the OS rarely knows job lengths—and the need for a scheduler like SJF/STCF without a priori knowledge, while also achieving good response time like RR. nodes.title: 7.9 No More Oracle

It summarizes two scheduling families: shortest job remaining for turnaround time and round-robin for response time, noting their trade-off. It introduces the multi-level feedback queue, which uses past behavior to predict future job lengths, as the next topic.

nodes.title: 7.10 Summary

nodes.title: 08 Scheduling - The Multi-Level Feedback Queue

nodes.summary: The chapter introduces the Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ) scheduler, created by Corbato et al. in 1962 for CTSS and refined for modern systems. It aims to optimize turnaround time and minimize response time without knowledge of job lengths. MLFQ uses multiple priority queues, varying job priorities based on observed behavior to predict future behavior. Basic rules are: higher priority runs, equal priority runs round-robin. The chapter includes a figure example and notes on learning from history.

nodes.title: TIP: LEARN FROM HISTORY
nodes.summary: The text introduces the multi-level feedback queue (MLFQ) as a scheduling system that learns from past job behavior to predict future execution, similar to hardware branch predictors and caching. It describes MLFQ's basic rules: multiple priority queues, with higher-priority jobs running first, and round-robin among equal priorities. Priorities are dynamically adjusted based on observed behavior—interactive jobs keep high priority, CPU-intensive jobs are demoted. Two fundamental rules are stated: Rule 1 (higher priority runs) and Rule 2 (equal priority runs in round-robin). A figure example shows jobs at different priority levels, but the static snapshot is noted as insufficient to illustrate MLFQ's dynamic nature.

nodes.title: 8.1 MLFQ: Basic Rules
nodes.summary: The text introduces Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ) scheduling, which learns from job history to predict future behavior, akin to OS techniques like branch predictors. MLFQ adjusts job priorities dynamically based on observed behavior, promoting interactive jobs and demoting CPU-intensive ones. An example of a single long-running job in a three-queue scheduler is mentioned.

nodes.title: 8.2 Attempt #1: How To Change Priority
nodes.summary: The text explains Multi-Level Feedback Queue scheduling: initial rules place new jobs at highest priority, demote jobs using full time slices, and keep jobs that yield early at the same priority. Examples show single long-running job, short interactive job approximating SJF, and I/O-bound job kept high priority. nodes.title: 8.3 Attempt #2: The Priority Boost

nodes.title: 8.4 Attempt #3: Better Accounting
nodes.summary: This text covers MLFQ scheduling improvements. It discusses priority boost with period S to prevent starvation, noting the difficulty of setting S. It addresses gaming via better accounting: Rule 4 demotes a job after it uses its total time allotment at a level, regardless of yielding, preventing I/O-based gaming. Tuning issues are examined: number of queues, time-slice sizes (short for high-priority interactive jobs, long for low-priority CPU-bound jobs), and boost frequency. nodes.title: 8.5 Tuning MLFQ And Other Issues
nodes.summary: The text explains MLFQ scheduling's anti-gaming Rule 4, which reduces priority once a job uses its total time allotment. nodes.title: 09 Scheduling - Proportional Share
CRUX: HOW TO SHARE THE CPU PROPORTIONALLY
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces proportional-share (fair-share) scheduling, which guarantees each job a percentage of CPU time rather than optimizing turnaround or response time. It highlights lottery scheduling as a modern example where tickets represent a process's resource share, with more tickets increasing the chance of winning a lottery held each time slice. The chapter poses the crux of how to design such a scheduler and its key mechanisms, then explains the basic concept of tickets, using an example of two processes with 75 and 25 tickets to illustrate probabilistic allocation of CPU proportionally.

nodes.title: 9.1 Basic Concept: Tickets Represent Your Share
key_items: TIP: USE TICKETS TO REPRESENT SHARES
nodes.summary: This chapter introduces proportional-share (fair-share) scheduling, which guarantees each job a percentage of CPU time rather than optimizing turnaround or response time. It uses lottery scheduling as an example, where tickets represent shares and a random lottery decides which process runs next, providing probabilistic correctness. The chapter covers basic concepts, ticket mechanisms like currency, transfer, and inflation, and highlights the use of randomness for robustness, light weight, and speed. It also includes examples and tips on using tickets to represent shares.

nodes.title: 9.2 Ticket Mechanisms
nodes.summary: The text explains proportional share scheduling using tickets to represent CPU shares, applicable to memory allocation. It details ticket mechanisms: currency for user-defined allocation converted to global values, transfer for temporarily handing tickets to another process, and inflation for trusted environments. Implementation is simple: use a random number generator, a process list, and total tickets. The algorithm traverses the list, summing tickets until exceeding the random winner, then schedules that process. An example with processes A, B, and C illustrates the decision code and suggests sorting by ticket count for efficiency.

nodes.title: 9.3 Implementation
nodes.summary: The text covers the implementation of lottery scheduling, including C code for making a scheduling decision by picking a random winning ticket, traversing a process list with a counter to find the winner, and an example with processes A, B, and C having 100, 50, and 250 tickets. It notes implementation simplicity, suggests sorting the list by ticket count for efficiency, and presents a fairness study with two equal-ticket jobs, defining unfairness metric U as the ratio of completion times and showing that unfairness decreases as job length increases.

nodes.title: 9.4 An Example
nodes.summary: The text discusses lottery scheduling fairness, presenting an unfairness metric U based on job completion times and plotting average unfairness against job length. It addresses the open problem of ticket assignment and introduces stride scheduling as a deterministic alternative. Stride scheduling uses a stride (inverse of tickets) and a pass value to select the process with the lowest pass, incrementing it by the stride each run. A pseudocode example with processes A, B, and C illustrates the algorithm, which achieves proportional share without randomness.

nodes.title: 9.5 How To Assign Tickets?
nodes.summary: The text addresses ticket assignment in lottery scheduling, noting the difficulty and the open problem of allocating tickets to jobs, with user-controlled allocation as a non-solution. It then introduces deterministic stride scheduling by Waldspurger, explaining stride calculation as inverse to tickets, pass values, and the algorithm: always run the process with lowest pass, then increment its pass by its stride. Pseudocode and an example with three processes illustrate the deterministic fair-share approach.

nodes.title: 9.6 Why Not Deterministic?
nodes.summary: This text covers proportional-share scheduling, focusing on ticket assignment challenges and deterministic stride scheduling. It explains stride scheduling using strides (inverse of tickets) and pass values, with pseudocode and a trace showing exact proportional CPU allocation. It contrasts lottery scheduling's probabilistic approach and lack of global state, which simplifies adding new jobs, with stride scheduling's precision. nodes.title: 9.7 Summary

nodes.title: CRUX: HOW TO SCHEDULE JOBS ON MULTIPLE CPUS

nodes.title: 10.1 Background: Multiprocessor Architecture

nodes.title: 10.2 Don’t Forget Synchronization
nodes.summary: The text discusses multiprocessor scheduling challenges, focusing on cache coherence and its hardware solution via bus snooping, while noting write-back cache complexity. nodes.title: 10.3 One Final Issue: Cache Affinity

nodes.title: 10.4 Single-Queue Scheduling

Single-queue multiprocessor scheduling (SQMS) reuses single-CPU scheduling but suffers from scalability due to lock contention and poor cache affinity, often requiring affinity mechanisms. nodes.title: 10.5 Multi-Queue Scheduling

nodes.title: 41 Locality and The Fast File System
Old UNIX File System and Its Poor Performance
nodes.summary: The page describes the old UNIX file system written by Ken Thompson, with data structures: super block (S), inodes, and data blocks. The super block held volume size, inode count, and free list pointer. Inodes stored file metadata, and data blocks held file contents. It supported files and directory hierarchy, advancing over record-based systems. However, performance was terrible, delivering only 2% of disk bandwidth, because the system treated the disk like random-access memory, spreading data without regard to expensive positioning costs, often causing seeks between inodes and data blocks.

nodes.title: 41.1 The Problem: Poor Performance

nodes.title: 41.2 FFS: Disk Awareness Is The Solution

nodes.title: 41.3 Organizing Structure: The Cylinder Group
nodes.summary: The Fast File System (FFS) introduced disk-aware design to improve performance while maintaining the same API. It organizes disks into cylinder groups (or block groups in modern systems) containing superblock, inode and data bitmaps, inodes, and data blocks. FFS places related files and directories together within groups using heuristics: directories are placed in groups with few directories and many free inodes; file data blocks are allocated in the same group as their inode; files in the same directory are placed in the directory's group. File creation involves updating multiple structures: inode bitmap, inode, data bitmap, data block, parent directory entry, and parent inode.

nodes.title: 41.5 Measuring File Locality

It analyzes trace data showing 7% repeated opens, 40% within same directory or file, and 25% at distance two, while noting FFS misses this two-level locality. A random trace serves as comparison. Finally, it describes the large-file exception, where FFS spreads a large file's blocks across multiple block groups after the direct pointers to preserve locality for related files.

nodes.title: 41.6 The Large-File Exception
nodes.summary: The text discusses FFS locality: SEER traces show 40% of file accesses are to same file or same directory, and 25% at distance two (e.g., src to obj), which FFS policies do not capture. It contrasts with random traces. Then, it explains the large-file exception: after 12 direct blocks, subsequent chunks are placed in different block groups to avoid filling one group, hurting sequential performance; chunk size is chosen via amortization (e.g., 409.6KB for 50% bandwidth). FFS used inode-based placement: direct blocks in same group, indirect blocks in separate groups. Finally, it introduces sub-blocks (512 bytes) to reduce internal fragmentation for small files.

nodes.title: 43 Log-structured File Systems
43 Log-structured File Systems (intro)

It emphasizes that details matter. An ideal file system focuses on write performance, sequential bandwidth, and RAID compatibility. LFS buffers all updates in memory segments and writes them sequentially to unused disk locations, never overwriting. The text also poses the crux: how to make all writes sequential, and begins explaining with an example of writing a data block.

nodes.title: Log-Structured File Systems: Sequential Writes and Details
key_items: THE CRUX: HOW TO MAKE ALL WRITES SEQUENTIAL WRITES?

nodes.title: 43.1 Writing To Disk Sequentially

nodes.title: 43.2 Writing Sequentially And Effectively

nodes.title: 43.3 How Much To Buffer?

nodes.title: 43.4 Problem: Finding Inodes

nodes.title: 43.5 Solution Through Indirection: The Inode Map

nodes.title: 43.6 Completing The Solution: The Checkpoint Region

nodes.title: 43.7 Reading A File From Disk: A Recap

nodes.title: 43.8 What About Directories?
nodes.summary: This text explains how LFS handles directories and the recursive update problem. Directories store name-to-inode mappings like classic UNIX. Creating a file involves writing new inode, data, and directory data/inode sequentially. The inode map (imap) tracks inode locations, avoiding recursive updates since directory entries never change when inodes move. The text also introduces garbage collection: LFS writes new versions of file data and inodes to new locations, leaving old versions as garbage. Examples show updated or appended blocks. LFS keeps only latest live versions and must periodically clean dead structures, unlike versioning file systems that retain old versions.

nodes.title: 43.9 A New Problem: Garbage Collection
nodes.summary: The text addresses garbage collection in log-structured file systems (LFS). It explains that LFS writes new versions of file structures, leaving old versions as garbage. Examples show how updates and appends create both live and dead blocks. It discusses that LFS could be versioning but instead cleans dead versions to free space. Cleaning is a form of garbage collection, done segment-by-segment to maintain large contiguous free space. The cleaning process reads M old segments, compacts live blocks into N new segments, and frees the old. Two problems arise: mechanism and policy. The mechanism for determining block liveness uses segment summary blocks containing inode number and offset, checking the imap and inode to see if the block address matches. If so, it's live; otherwise, dead.

nodes.title: 43.10 Determining Block Liveness
nodes.summary: LFS cleaning frees old segments by reading partially-used segments, compacting live blocks into fewer new segments, and freeing old ones. Block liveness is determined via segment summary blocks that record inode number and offset, checked against the imap and inode; version numbers provide a shortcut. Policies decide when to clean (periodically, during idle time, or when full) and which segments to clean, with the original LFS segregating hot and cold segments to clean cold ones sooner, though later work improves on this.

nodes.title: I[k] imap
nodes.summary: The text describes how log-structured file systems determine block liveness using segment summaries and the imap, with a diagram showing a segment summary recording that data block A0 belongs to file k at offset 0, verified via the imap and inode. It then addresses cleaning policies: when to clean (periodically, during idle time, or when disk is full) and which blocks to clean, discussing the original LFS approach of segregating hot and cold segments—waiting longer to clean hot segments and cleaning cold segments sooner—and noting that later research improved on this heuristic.

nodes.title: 43.11 A Policy Question: Which Blocks To Clean, And When?

nodes.title: 43.12 Crash Recovery And The Log

For segment writes, LFS recovers by reading the last consistent CR, but to avoid losing recent updates, it employs a roll-forward technique to rebuild segments from the log. It introduces the NFSv2 protocol, focusing on the file handle (volume ID, inode number, generation number) for unique file identification. Key protocol messages are outlined, including LOOKUP, READ, WRITE, GETATTR, and others for file operations. The text details how the protocol supports POSIX API calls by translating client requests into stateless messages, with the client tracking open files and file pointers. It also describes the LOOKUP process for path resolution and the importance of self-contained requests for server crash recovery.

nodes.title: 48.6 From Protocol to Distributed File System
nodes.summary: The text explains NFS protocol operations including READ, WRITE, and GETATTR, detailing how a client-side file system translates application requests into protocol messages, tracks open files and file descriptors, maps to NFS file handles, manages file offsets, and sends LOOKUP requests for path traversal. It describes server responses needing all information for stateless operation. It then covers handling server failure using idempotent operations, where clients retry requests after timeouts because LOOKUP, READ, and WRITE are idempotent, ensuring reliable crash recovery.

nodes.title: 48.7 Handling Server Failure with Idempotent Operations
nodes.summary: The text discusses Sun's NFS and idempotency's role in handling server failures. It explains that when a client doesn't receive a reply due to lost messages or server crashes, NFSv2 clients retry requests because most operations, like LOOKUP, READ, and WRITE, are idempotent—repeating them has the same effect as once. This allows uniform handling of three loss cases: request lost, server down, or reply lost. However, non-idempotent operations like MKDIR can cause issues when retried after a lost reply, as the operation may succeed initially but fail on retry.

This section explains why servers crash due to power outages, software bugs, memory leaks, and network partitions, introducing Sun's NFS as an open protocol for interoperable multi-vendor systems. nodes.title: 49 The Andrew File System (AFS)
49.1 AFS Version 1
nodes.summary: The text introduces the Andrew File System (AFS), developed at Carnegie-Mellon University in the 1980s by M. Satyanarayanan, focusing on scalability. It contrasts AFS with NFS in protocol design and cache consistency, highlighting AFS's whole-file caching on local disk. AFSv1, originally the ITC distributed file system, used Venus client and Vice server, with protocol messages like Fetch, Store, TestAuth, GetFileStat, and ListDir. It cached entire files locally, with read/write operations local, and only flushed modified files on close. Problems with AFSv1 led to a redesign, as discussed in the next section.

nodes.title: 49.2 Problems with Version 1
nodes.summary: The text details the Andrew File System (AFS) protocol, starting with AFSv1 operations (TestAuth, GetFileStat, Fetch, Store, SetFileStat, ListDir) and its whole-file caching on client disk and memory, contrasting with NFS block caching. It notes AFSv1's problems: high path-traversal costs and excessive TestAuth messages, plus load imbalance and per-client processes. Patterson's Law is highlighted. AFSv2 improvements include callbacks to reduce client-server interactions and file identifiers (FIDs) instead of pathnames, with clients walking paths and caching directories.

nodes.title: 49.3 Improving the Protocol
key_items: THE CRUX: HOW TO DESIGN A SCALABLE FILE PROTOCOL
nodes.summary: The text addresses AFS scalability issues where servers became bottlenecks and overloaded with TestAuth messages. It poses the crux of designing a scalable file protocol to minimize server interactions. AFSv2 solutions include callbacks, where servers promise to notify clients of cached file modifications, reducing client-server interactions. It also introduces File Identifiers (FIDs) with volume ID, file ID, and uniquifier, replacing pathnames. Clients walk pathnames incrementally, caching directory contents and setting callbacks at each step, as illustrated with /home/remzi/notes.txt, reducing server load compared to NFS.

nodes.title: 49.4 AFS Version 2
nodes.summary: AFSv2 addresses scalability by using callbacks so servers notify clients of file changes, eliminating repeated validity checks, and by using file identifiers (FIDs) instead of pathnames, letting clients cache and traverse directories locally. The text details a sample file-open sequence with callbacks, contrasts polling versus interrupts, and covers cache consistency: updates become visible and callbacks break when a file is closed across machines, while same-machine writes are immediately visible. 49.5 Cache Consistency

It details AFS's cache consistency mechanisms: updates become visible and callbacks invalidate caches when a file is closed on different machines, while same-machine writes are immediately visible. It describes the last-writer-wins approach for concurrent cross-machine modifications and contrasts it with NFS's block-based protocol. Crash recovery is more complex than NFS, requiring clients to validate caches after server or client reboots. nodes.title: 49.6 Crash Recovery

nodes.title: I. Flash-based SSDs
I. 1 Storing a Single Bit
nodes.summary: This text introduces flash-based SSDs as persistent storage with no moving parts, unlike HDDs, and retaining data without power. It focuses on NAND flash, invented by Fujio Masuoka, highlighting challenges: erasing larger blocks before writing pages and wear from repeated writes. It covers storing bits in SLC, MLC, and TLC flash, with terminology tips. Flash chips are organized into banks/planes containing blocks (128-256 KB) and pages (4 KB), and the critical erasure-before-write constraint is emphasized for SSD construction.

nodes.title: I. 2 From Bits to Banks/Planes
nodes.summary: The text discusses flash-based SSDs, emphasizing terminology differences for blocks and pages across domains and advising memorization. It covers flash chip organization into banks/planes with blocks (128KB-256KB) and pages (few KB), and the critical constraint that writing requires erasing an entire block first. It details three low-level operations: read (fast, random access), erase (slow, resets block to 1s), and program (moderate speed, writes page). It explains page states: INVALID, ERASED, VALID, with transitions via erase and program, noting pages cannot be reprogrammed without erasing the block. Examples illustrate state changes.

nodes.title: I. 3 Basic Flash Operations
nodes.summary: This section explains basic flash operations: read, erase, and program. Read accesses any page quickly, making flash a random-access device. Erase resets an entire block to 1s, destroying data, and is expensive. Program writes a page by changing 1s to 0s, but only after erasing the block, and is slower than read. Pages have states: INVALID, ERASED, and VALID. Reprogramming requires erasing the whole block, which affects all pages. A detailed example shows that writing one page necessitates erasing the block, losing other pages' data unless moved. The summary notes reading is fast, writing is costly and causes wear, impacting SSD design.

nodes.title: A Detailed Example
nodes.summary: This text explains flash-based SSDs with a detailed example of writing to a 4-page block. It shows that writing requires erasing the entire block first, which erases all pages, so data must be moved before overwriting. It summarizes that reading is fast, but writing is expensive and causes wear out, impacting SSD design for performance and reliability.

nodes.title: Summary
Summary (intro)
nodes.summary: The text explains flash-based SSD write operations via a detailed example: to overwrite a page, the entire block must be erased first, requiring valuable data to be moved elsewhere, as erasing destroys all pages in the block. It summarizes that reading is fast, writing is expensive and causes wear out. It then provides raw flash performance characteristics (read, program, erase latencies for SLC, MLC, TLC), discusses reliability concerns like wear out (rated P/E cycles: 10,000 for MLC, 100,000 for SLC) and disturbance (read/program disturbs), and notes that write performance and reliability are central to SSD design.

nodes.title: I. 4 Flash Performance And Reliability
key_items: TIP: THE IMPORTANCE OF BACKWARDS COMPATIBILITY
nodes.summary: This text summarizes flash-based SSDs, starting with raw flash performance characteristics across SLC, MLC, and TLC types, including read, program, and erase latencies. It discusses reliability concerns: wear-out due to limited program/erase cycles, disturbance issues like read/program disturbs, and varying block lifetimes. A tip emphasizes backwards compatibility in layered systems, citing Sun ZFS as an example. It then explains transforming raw flash into SSDs, covering internal components (flash chips, volatile memory, control logic) and the flash translation layer (FTL) that maps logical to physical operations, aiming for performance via parallelism and reduced write amplification.

nodes.title: I. 5 From Raw Flash to Flash-Based SSDs
nodes.summary: The text covers backwards compatibility in layered systems, citing stable interfaces in OS APIs, disk blocks, and IP networking, but notes potential rigidity, exemplified by Sun ZFS redesign. It then explains flash-based SSDs, detailing their components: flash chips, volatile memory, control logic, and the Flash Translation Layer (FTL) that maps logical block reads/writes to physical flash operations. Performance goals include using multiple chips in parallel and reducing write amplification. Reliability focuses on wear leveling and sequential programming to mitigate wear out and program disturbance. Finally, it describes a direct-mapped FTL as a bad approach due to severe write amplification, poor performance, and rapid wear out from uneven writes.

nodes.title: I. 6 FTL Organization: A Bad Approach
nodes.summary: This text describes flash-based SSDs, covering host interface logic, memory, flash controller, and flash components via a logical diagram. It discusses FTL challenges: write amplification, reliability, wear leveling, and program disturbance. The direct-mapped FTL approach is critiqued for poor performance and reliability due to excessive wear. The log-structured FTL is introduced, where writes are appended and a mapping table tracks physical addresses, with an example of write operations and block states.

nodes.title: I. 7 A Log-Structured FTL
nodes.summary: This text explains log-structured flash translation layers (FTLs) for flash-based SSDs. It describes the basic logging mechanism where writes are appended to free pages and a mapping table tracks logical-to-physical addresses. An example shows sequential writes, block erasure, and mapping updates. The benefits include improved performance, reliability, and wear leveling. The aside discusses mapping table persistence via out-of-band areas and recovery challenges. Downsides include garbage creation from overwrites and high memory cost of mapping tables. Garbage collection is then introduced, with a continued example showing overwrites creating invalid pages and the need to reclaim dead blocks.

nodes.title: ASIDE: FTL MAPPING INFORMATION PERSISTENCE
nodes.summary: The text explains FTL mapping persistence in flash SSDs, covering power-loss recovery via out-of-band areas or logging. It details garbage collection (GC) for reclaiming dead blocks, including the process of reading live pages and erasing blocks, plus overprovisioning to reduce GC costs. It also addresses mapping table size issues, comparing page-level and block-level FTL, noting block-based mapping's write amplification problem for small writes and the logical address structure.

The section covers flash-based SSD write operations, requiring block erasure before overwriting pages, which moves valid data and causes wear. It details raw flash performance latencies for SLC, MLC, and TLC, and reliability concerns like wear-out (P/E cycles) and disturbance. It explains transforming raw flash into SSDs via the Flash Translation Layer (FTL), including components, performance via parallelism and reduced write amplification, and reliability through wear leveling. It critiques direct-mapped FTL for write amplification and introduces log-structured FTL, discussing benefits, mapping table persistence, garbage collection, overprovisioning, and block-level mapping trade-offs.

nodes.title: Block-Based Mapping
nodes.summary: The text covers flash-based SSD optimizations: overprovisioning to reduce garbage collection costs by adding extra flash capacity for background cleaning and increased internal bandwidth. It then addresses mapping table size issues, explaining that page-level FTL is impractical due to large memory needs. Block-based mapping reduces mapping overhead but causes performance problems with small writes, illustrated with an example. Hybrid mapping is introduced as a solution, using a small log table with per-page mappings for log blocks and a larger data table with per-block mappings, periodically compacting log blocks to keep them small, with examples showing mapping updates.

nodes.title: Hybrid Mapping
key_items: I. 10 Wear Leveling; I. 11 SSD Performance And Cost
nodes.summary: The text covers hybrid mapping in flash-based SSDs, where FTLs use log blocks with per-page mappings and data blocks with per-block mappings. It explains switch, partial, and full merges to convert log blocks, detailing their processes and impact on write amplification. Wear leveling is described as spreading erase/program cycles evenly, with garbage collection and data rewriting to prevent uneven wear. SSD performance is compared to HDDs, highlighting SSDs' superior random I/O performance due to no mechanical components, with supporting data.

nodes.title: Performance
nodes.summary: The text covers wear leveling in flash-based SSDs, explaining how FTLs evenly distribute write/erase cycles to prevent premature block failure, using log-structuring and garbage collection, and periodically relocating long-lived data, which increases write amplification and reduces performance. It then compares SSD performance and cost to HDDs: SSDs excel at random I/O but have less advantage in sequential I/O, with random writes sometimes outperforming random reads due to log-structured design. Cost-wise, SSDs are over 10x more expensive per GB. These differences drive storage system design, favoring SSDs for performance and HDDs for capacity, with hybrid approaches for mixed workloads.

nodes.title: Cost
nodes.summary: The text presents a performance and cost comparison between SSDs and hard drives, highlighting SSDs' superior random I/O performance, comparable sequential performance, and the impact of log-structured design on random writes. It discusses cost per GB, favoring HDDs for large-scale storage, and suggests hybrid systems. The summary section notes SSDs' growing prevalence and recommends further reading on device performance, FTL design, distributed systems, and practical information from the popular press, including TLC/SLC usage and recent surveys.
